content: The first study conducted in Ethiopia was an evaluation trial aimed at trachoma elimination. Incidentally, it demonstrated a reduction in childhood mortality within the intervention communities. The second study, conducted across Malawi, Niger, and Tanzania, was a large-scale, rigorously conducted cluster-randomized controlled trial (rCT) designed to assess the impact of the intervention on mortality. The third study focused on seasonal malaria chemoprevention (SMC) in malaria-endemic regions. The WHO Guideline on mass drug administration (MDA) of azithromycin to children under five years of age to promote child survival considered the results of these three studies separately. Subgroup analysis of the second study revealed a significant reduction in mortality in Niger but not in the other two countries. The third study failed to find any significant difference in the risk of hospitalization or mortality. Due to these inconsistencies and the heterogeneity of the studies, the quality of evidence was graded as low. Two studies included infants under one year of age, and subgroup analyses were conducted to evaluate the intervention's effects on age-specific mortality (<1 year vs. 1–5 years). However, confidence intervals for these groups overlapped, indicating uncertainty in the findings. One study compared mortality risk with different azithromycin regimens, focusing on deaths secondary to acute respiratory infections (ARI), febrile illnesses, malaria, and other infectious causes. Two other studies reported that infection-related deaths accounted for 40–71% of total deaths but did not provide separate details on infection-related mortality in the two groups. Regarding morbidity, two cohort studies and two cluster-randomized controlled trials examined the effects of MDA-azithromycin on ARI incidence. These studies, conducted in Nepal, Tanzania, Gambia, Mali, and Burkina Faso, showed no reduction in ARI risk with MDA-azithromycin. The quality of evidence was graded as low. Similarly, four studies investigating diarrhea incidence also graded the evidence as low. For malaria, two studies—one observational study in Tanzania and one rCT in Mali and Burkina Faso—reported on malaria incidence, with the quality of evidence graded as very low. Hospitalizations were reported in only one multi-country rCT conducted in Mali and Burkina Faso. Malaria was the most common cause of hospitalization (72%). The quality of evidence for this outcome was also graded as very low. A systematic literature search was conducted to identify clinical evidence on the impact of MDA-azithromycin on antimicrobial resistance (AMR). The search included studies published between 1997 and 2019, focusing on children aged 1–59 months or their household contacts, primarily in the African region. Interventions included MDA with azithromycin, clarithromycin, or erythromycin at intervals of up to 12 months. A total of 26 articles were identified, with 18 meeting inclusion criteria for final analysis. The impact of MDA-azithromycin on the carriage of resistant gut bacteria was evaluated. One rCT in Tanzania showed that single MDA-azithromycin treatments substantially increased macrolide-resistant E. coli. Younger age and previous diarrhea were associated with higher odds of resistance carriage, likely due to increased exposure to environmental strains via fecal-oral transmission. Resistance carriage decreased over time but remained elevated above baseline levels six months after dosing. Underlying resistance genes may persist. The trial by Doan et al., nested within the MORDOR study, reported an increase in macrolide genetic determinants in the gut of preschool children after four biannual azithromycin treatments compared to placebo. This finding suggests that selective pressure from distributed treatments increased macrolide resistance. However, resistance to non-macrolide antibiotics was not significantly different between MDA and placebo groups. Regarding nasopharyngeal bacteria, studies in Nepal and Tanzania showed no substantial development of macrolide resistance in S. pneumoniae six to twelve months after a single MDA-azithromycin dose, especially in areas with low baseline resistance prevalence. Even after repeated annual mass treatments, pneumococcal macrolide resistance did not exceed 5% six months after a second treatment. However, studies with multiple MDA rounds reported sharp rises in azithromycin-resistant pneumococcal isolates, peaking at up to 80% shortly after treatment, though resistance rates declined after cessation of MDA. In Gambia, three MDA-azithromycin rounds were associated with a short-term increase in nasopharyngeal azithromycin-resistant or macrolide-inducible clindamycin-resistant S. aureus. Resistance rates dropped after MDA cessation but did not return to baseline levels. Studies have not demonstrated persistent resistance development in nasopharyngeal S. pneumoniae to penicillin after MDA. However, increased cotrimoxazole resistance is common, and cross-resistance with sulfadoxine/pyrimethamine has been described. The gut microbiome, a reservoir for antibiotic resistance genes, may be disturbed by antibiotic exposure, selecting for resistant microbes. A study in Niger using 16S rRNA gene sequencing showed that azithromycin reduced intestinal microbial diversity five days after treatment. Community-level alterations, such as reduced microbiome richness, were observed in the treatment group compared to placebo. Antibiotic-induced microbiota alterations, including resistant strains, may persist even after treatment cessation. Most studies focused on individual-level resistance impacts, with limited information on population-level effects. Exposed children eventually return to the non-exposed population, but the long-term implications of MDA-azithromycin on antimicrobial resistance remain a concern.
